cells.tense: You're here, tending it, and the weight is being borne.
cells.verb: keeping two living things alive at once, with care instead of force
cells.place: in the part of you that carries what has to be carried
cells.ask: Let one person see what the tending has cost you, and let one thing that's done be done — so that putting it down feels like finishing, not giving up.
cells.core:
You're here, tending it, and the weight is being borne. There are two things that both need you, and you haven't dropped either one or turned either into a fight — you keep them going by paying attention, not by gripping. That's what's holding you up: not hardness, but the steady work of keeping things alive.

None of this requires anyone to notice. But it could feed something, if you let it: one person seeing what this carrying actually costs, and one piece of it that's finished being allowed to be finished. Setting it down that way isn't losing it. It's what completion looks like.
cells.sheetLine: You keep two things alive at once, and it's holding you up.

cells.tense: You're bracing for a season that hasn't arrived.
cells.verb: tending everything before it needs you
cells.place: in the part of you that carries what has to be carried
cells.ask: Picture one thing you've cared for that already came up and stayed up, and let yourself feel how good that is — long enough that the care stops exhausting you and the holding loosens its grip.
cells.core:
You're bracing for a season that hasn't arrived. Every demand on you gets tended ahead of time — watered before it's dry, propped before it's leaning — because somewhere out ahead there's a shortfall you're already answering. The carrying has turned into clutching, and clutching is what makes it heavy.

So stop looking forward for a minute and look at what's grown. One thing you tended that came up and stayed up. Sit with how that actually feels, finished and real. That satisfaction is where the grip comes loose — care that doesn't wear you out, holding without squeezing.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending a shortfall that hasn't happened yet.

cells.tense: You stopped tending somewhere behind you, and you're still standing there.
cells.verb: letting what grows go untended while you keep carrying
cells.place: in the part of you that carries what has to be carried
cells.ask: Name one thing you still hope comes of all this, and take one step toward it this week — not toward the chores, toward the hope — so that something you planted gets to show, and the care comes back without forcing.
cells.core:
You stopped tending somewhere behind you, and you're still standing there. There was a time when caring for it didn't save it, and some part of you decided the carrying would go on but the tending wouldn't. So you're still bearing the load — you haven't put it down — but nothing in it is being looked after. It's weight without a garden.

Don't try to tend harder; that well is dry right now. Go around it instead. There's something you still hope will come of all this — you'd know it if asked. Say what it is and move toward it, once. Hope is what refills the care, not duty. And when something you planted finally shows, the tending comes back on its own.
cells.sheetLine: You're still carrying it. You just stopped looking after it.

cells.tense: You're already the one keeping it all alive, and you call it getting by.
cells.verb: quietly tending two things at once
cells.place: in the part of you that carries what has to be carried
cells.ask: Tell one person plainly what you've been giving up to keep this going and what it's for — so that the work gets its name back, and what's done can be set down as finished rather than dropped.
cells.core:
You're already the one keeping it all alive, and you call it getting by. Two things depend on you and both are still standing, because you've been tending them — choosing what gets your attention, holding both without letting either fall. But if someone asked, you'd say it just worked out. The care is running. Nobody, including you, has said whose it is.

The way back is simpler than it sounds. One person, told plainly: here's what I've been giving up to keep this going, and here's what it's for. Not for praise — so the work has a name and an owner. Once it does, the parts that are finished can be set down as finished. That's not dropping them. That's what completing something feels like when you admit you did it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already tending it. You just haven't called it yours.
